newsitem.title: USA: General Re Q1 helped by property, health.
newsitem.headline: General Re Q1 helped by property, health.

text.p: General Re Corp's first-quarter operating profits rose more than 12 percent, helped by property-casualty underwriting, improved worldwide life-health results and good results at General Re Financial Products.
General Re reported operating profits of $2.90 a share compared with the First Call consensus estimate of $2.85 a share. The company posted operating profits of $2.58 a share a year ago.
"Both the North American and international insurance markets remain very competitive," General Re chief executive Ronald Ferguson said in a statement.
"We continue to maintain our underwriting discipline as we pursue new business opportunities in this difficult environment," he said.
The underwriting combined ratio for the North American property-casualty operations was 99.2 percent in the first quarter compared with 98.9 percent a year ago.
The first quarter was not significantly impacted by catastrophes in either year, the company said.
North American property-casualty premiums written rose 15.3 percent to $795 million in the first quarter.
Net premiums relating to the acquisition of National Re Corp contributed about $84 million in the quarter.
Excluding the National Re business, North American traditional premiums rose 4.1 percent in the first quarter.
Non-traditional premiums written in the first quarter fell 4.0 percent from a year ago and comprised about 10.5 percent of the total North American property-casualty premiums written in the period.
The international property/casualty combined ratio in the first quarter rose to 103.5 percent from 101.7 percent a year ago.
International property-casualty results are reported on a one-quarter lag.
The underwriting result for the 1997 first quarter includes two large individual property losses.
International property-casualty net premiums written fell 10.2 percent to $468 million in the first quarter.

Excluding the effect of exchange rate fluctuations and the runoff business from Cologne Re's United States property-casualty subsidiary, international property-casualty traditional premiums written were flat in the quarter.
Life-health pretax operating income rose to $28 million in the first quarter from $12 million in the same period of 1996.
Life-health results are also reported on a one quarter lag.
The increase in operating income compared to recent prior quarters was primarily due to better mortality experience in the United States.
Worldwide life-health net premiums written rose 18.8 percent to $298 million in the first quarter of 1997.
Growth was achieved in various markets, including the United States, Europe and Australia, General Re said.
Financial Services had first quarter operating revenues of $82 million, up 29.8 percent.
Pretax operating income rose to $30 million from $25 million in the prior year.
